summary: The revision builds on the founder's real skills: a read-only M365 monitor, external scans and a manual pen test. Three months is plausible for the monitor, WISP generator and reports. Remaining risks: the app becomes a credential vault into many financial tenants, Exchange checks need a directory role in each tenant, signals depend on licence, the partner console inflates scope, and the ~8 h/client budget understates testing.

objections.objection: Holding admin-consented application permissions (AuditLog.Read.All, Directory/Policy read, MailboxSettings read, Exchange.ManageAsApp) for dozens of financial-firm tenants makes one app secret or certificate a key to all of them. Read-only scopes still expose inbox rules, sign-in logs and the full user directory, which is exactly the reconnaissance a BEC attacker wants. The revision names vendor security as a hardest part but does not design it: certificate-only credentials in an HSM or Key Vault, per-tenant token isolation, no standing human access, and a 314.4(f)-ready security program. A solo founder has to build this to production quality inside the same three months.

Graph does not expose external forwarding settings (mailbox ForwardingSmtpAddress, remote-domain auto-forward, outbound spam policy). These need Exchange Online PowerShell app-only access, which requires Exchange.ManageAsApp plus a Microsoft Entra directory role assigned to the app's service principal in each client tenant, with certificate authentication and a PowerShell runtime in the backend. That is a per-tenant onboarding step beyond one-click admin consent, and small-office owners or wary MSPs may refuse it. It also complicates a Python/Graph-only backend.

Signal coverage varies by licence. Risky users and risk detections need Entra ID P2, which few 3-20-seat offices have. Sign-in log and registration-detail reports are tied to premium tiers, so they may be missing on Business Basic or Standard tenants. MFA coverage then has to fall back to per-user authentication-method enumeration and a check on security defaults or conditional access. The concept names this risk, but the MVP needs a per-SKU check matrix and test tenants for each SKU before launch, or the monthly evidence quietly varies by client.

Founder hours are underestimated. An annual pen test of external services plus an M365 tenant (scoping, written authorization, testing, retest, report), two scans with triage, a tabletop and an annual report will not fit in about 8 hours per client unless the test is a templated tool run. A templated run risks not counting as 'penetration testing' under 314.4(d)(2). At a realistic 15-25 hours, 40 clients needs 600-1,000 hours a year beside running the platform.

A white-label multi-client MSP partner console in the v1 feature list adds multi-level tenancy (MSP > client > users), role-based access, branding and report theming. That is scope creep for a three-month solo MVP. Defer it, and serve the first MSP partners with exported PDFs.

Multi-tenant apps from unverified publishers face consent warnings and blocks. Microsoft publisher verification (a partner program ID and a verified domain) and a stable consent flow should be done before outreach, or the first admin consents will stall.

strongest_point: The scope is now small and squarely within the founder's skills: read-only Graph checks, external scanning and manual testing, with no reportability engine, legal tables or client-side scripts.
what_would_change_my_mind: A working prototype that onboards 3 real tenants (Business Basic, Standard and Premium) with one consent flow and returns MFA, forwarding and admin-role findings on each, with the Exchange role step timed and accepted

A written vendor security design (certificate-only app credentials in a managed key store, per-tenant isolation, audit log, MFA, no standing access) reviewed by an outside tester before the first client connects
Time logs from 3 pilot pen tests plus scans showing 10 h or less per client, with a report format that a lawyer or insurer accepts as 314.4(d)(2) evidence
The partner console moved to post-MVP, and the MVP feature list confirmed to fit in 3 months by a week-level plan

resolved_prior.objection: Program omitted 314.4(d)(2) scanning/testing and the 5,000-consumer branching
resolved_prior.note: Six-monthly scans, annual pen test and onboarding scoping by the 314.6 threshold now in MVP and pricing tiers; delivery hours remain underestimated (new objection).

resolved_prior.objection: Lawyer-reviewed reportability tree and 50-state table outside the one-month plan
resolved_prior.note: Both removed from scope; the first-hour card hands off to counsel or the insurer, which takes the content burden off the critical path.

resolved_prior.objection: App holds sensitive client data and needs its own security program; out-of-band incident access
resolved_prior.note: Data held is narrower (no SSNs, returns or mail content) and months_to_mvp went from 1 to 3, but the app now holds standing read access to many tenants. The security design is still only named as a hard part. Out-of-band access matters less now that the incident card is static.

resolved_prior.objection: No API for FTC submission or desktop tax software
resolved_prior.note: FTC pre-fill dropped; inventory now comes mainly from M365 Graph rather than tax software.

resolved_prior.objection: PowerShell hardening scripts risk lockouts across mixed configurations
resolved_prior.note: Scripts removed; fixes go to the firm's IT person or MSP, and founder changes need a separate written authorization.

resolved_prior.objection: Bursty incident support overwhelms a solo founder
resolved_prior.note: No incident hours are sold; the card hands off to the insurer and counsel. The burst risk has moved to testing season (see the hours objection).
